| --- | --- |

title: Domestic output and national income — Caldin
stem: All values and places are constructed. In Caldin, nominal GDP is 450 billion crowns, factor income received from abroad is 28 billion and factor income paid abroad is 40 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate GNI.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why GDP and GNI differ.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain one limitation of using either figure alone to assess welfare.

steps.text: Net factor income received from abroad=28−40=-12 billion crowns.
438 billion crowns.
GDP measures production within the territory.
GNI measures income accruing to resident factors.
Here net outward factor income makes GNI lower than GDP.
The aggregate does not reveal income distribution, unpaid work or environmental damage.
For example, higher total income can coexist with gains concentrated among a small group, so welfare is not fully captured.

title: The business cycle and unused resources — Ilyra
subtopic: The business cycle and unused resources
stem:
All values and places are constructed. In Ilyra, real GDP is falling below its long-run trend and factories reduce shifts as orders decline.

Answer parts (a)–(c) using the initial scenario. For part (d) only, consider the following additional evidence, which may change an initial assumption.

Additional application evidence: Potential output is unchanged during the contraction.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Distinguish a cyclical contraction from a fall in productive potential.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the likely employment effect.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why recovery need not initially cause rapid inflation.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how the additional evidence changes or qualifies the economic interpretation in this case.

steps.text: A cyclical contraction is a decline in actual real output.
Potential may remain intact if labour, capital and technology have not been lost.
Weaker orders reduce firms' demand for labour.
Some workers lose hours or jobs.
This is cyclical unemployment arising from weak aggregate demand, rather than automatically a skills mismatch.
The economy has spare capacity.
Firms can use idle labour and machinery to meet higher demand.
Price pressure may be limited until bottlenecks or full-capacity constraints become binding.
Identify the economic determinant, constraint or model assumption affected by this evidence, distinguishing it from the conditions used in the initial analysis.
The fall in activity is a larger negative output gap rather than necessarily a fall in productive capacity. A justified causal link is required for this explanation mark.

steps.text: More productive capital and more efficient logistics raise productivity.
The economy can produce more at full employment with its resources.

subject: economics
title: Unemployment and labour-force measurement — Quorin
stem: All values and places are constructed. In Quorin, the labour force is 800 thousand people, of whom 56 thousand are unemployed, available and actively seeking work. Another 20 thousand want jobs but have stopped looking.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the measured unemployment rate.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how discouraged workers affect interpretation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Distinguish structural from cyclical unemployment.

steps.text: Use 56 thousand actively seeking unemployed and the stated 800 thousand labour force; exclude the 20 thousand discouraged workers from the measure.
Those no longer searching are outside the stated labour-force definition.
They are not included in either the numerator or denominator of this rate.
The measured rate can therefore understate wider labour underutilization.
Structural unemployment arises from a mismatch of worker skills/location and available jobs.
Cyclical unemployment results from deficient aggregate demand during a downturn.

subtopic: Inflation, disinflation and the price level
stem: All values and places are constructed. In Selven, the consumer price index rises from 120 to 124.80. Last year's inflation rate was 7%.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the current inflation rate.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain whether the data show deflation or disinflation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain one distributional effect of unexpected inflation.

steps.text: Index-point change=124.80−120=4.80.
Disinflation.
Inflation slows from 7% to 4%.
The general price level is still rising, so this is not deflation.
Fixed nominal incomes or fixed nominal loan repayments lose real purchasing power.
For example borrowers with fixed nominal repayments may gain at lenders' expense; contracts indexed to inflation differ.

title: Real and nominal interest rates — Ulara
stem: All values and places are constructed. In Ulara, the nominal annual interest rate is 6% and expected inflation is 4%. Use the approximate real-interest-rate relationship.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the expected real interest rate.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why expected inflation matters for borrowing decisions.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain one limit to using low interest rates to increase investment.

steps.text: Real interest≈6−4.
Borrowers compare repayment cost with expected purchasing power and returns.
Higher expected inflation reduces a given nominal rate's real cost.
This can encourage interest-sensitive spending, other things equal; confidence and credit access still matter.
Firms may have pessimistic expected sales or high debt.
Even cheap credit will not make an unprofitable project attractive.
The response therefore depends on confidence and balance sheets rather than the interest rate alone.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the schedule is progressive.

steps.text: Tax on the 20-thousand middle band=4 thousand crowns.
Tax on income above 30 thousand=0.40×(40−30)=4 thousand.
Total tax=8 thousand crowns.
Average tax rate=8/40×100.
The average rate applies to the whole income; the marginal rate applies to the next unit of income.
The average tax rate rises as taxable income increases across these bands.
Higher earners pay a larger proportion of their income; the tax is not calculated by applying 40% to all income.

subject: economics
title: A downturn in a manufacturing economy — Arden
subtopic: A downturn in a manufacturing economy
stem:
All values and descriptions are fictional, constructed for practice. Arden: Factory orders decline after overseas customers cut spending. Real output falls below capacity; the government considers temporary maintenance projects, while some firms are heavily indebted.

The following accounting data relate to the same year.

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Nominal GDP (billion crowns) | 660 |
| GDP deflator (base year=100) | 110 |
| Population (million) | 20 |

Show working. Give exact answers or round to two decimal places, retaining units.

A further case detail: The public budget is tight and service providers cannot expand capacity immediately.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt:
(i) Define real GDP. [2]

(ii) Define unemployment. [2]

parts.label: b
parts.prompt:
(i) Calculate real GDP. [2]

(ii) Calculate real GDP per capita in crowns per person. [3]

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using an AD/AS diagram, explain the effect of weaker export demand.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why GDP and GNI may differ.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Using a diagram, explain how maintenance-project spending may affect output.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Explain one limit of interest-rate cuts in this case.

parts.label: g
parts.prompt: Using the information and your knowledge of economics, evaluate temporary government maintenance spending as a response to the downturn.

steps.text: Value of final domestic output adjusted for price-level changes.
It is measured at constant/base-year prices.
People without work who are available for employment.
They are actively seeking work under the stated labour-force measure.
600 billion crowns at base-year prices.
600 billion / 20 million.
Convert billion/million to 1000 crowns per person.
30 000 crowns per person.
Label price level/real output and AD1/AD2/SRAS.
Shift AD left, lowering output and the price level.
Exports are a component of aggregate demand.
Weaker output reduces firms' labour demand and can cause cyclical unemployment.
GDP concerns output inside the territory.
GNI concerns income accruing to resident factors.
Income paid to foreign owners is deducted in moving from GDP to GNI.
Income received by residents from foreign production is added.
Label AD1/AD2, SRAS and both macro axes.
Shift AD right.
Government final expenditure raises demand directly.
With spare capacity, firms can raise output; effects depend on leakages and confidence.
Some firms are heavily indebted.
Weak expected sales discourage new borrowing.
Lower borrowing costs may therefore generate little new investment.
The transmission depends on balance sheets and confidence.

Indicative model reasoning (not an additive checklist): Use declining orders, spare capacity and debt to compare fiscal support with rate cuts. Maintenance can be timely and preserve useful assets, but imports, procurement and temporary-job design affect output and durability. Weigh fiscal opportunity cost and the risk of continuing support after recovery.
Variant-specific evaluation: Timing, opportunity cost and short-run supply constraints qualify the scale of benefits.

subject: economics
title: Tourism recovery and capacity pressure — Hesper
stem:
All values and descriptions are fictional, constructed for practice. Hesper: Overseas visitor demand recovers rapidly after a quiet period. Hotels initially have spare rooms, but later skilled staff and airport capacity become scarce. The authority is considering advertising grants.

The following accounting data relate to the same year.

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Nominal GDP (billion crowns) | 726 |
| GDP deflator (base year=100) | 110 |
| Population (million) | 22 |

Show working. Give exact answers or round to two decimal places, retaining units.

A further case detail: Administrative records omit some low-income or remote households.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt:
(i) Define real GDP. [2]

(ii) Define unemployment. [2]

parts.label: b
parts.prompt:
(i) Calculate real GDP. [2]

(ii) Calculate real GDP per capita in crowns per person. [3]

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using an AD/AS diagram, explain the initial recovery in visitor spending.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why inflation pressure may become stronger later.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Using a PPC or LRAS diagram, explain the effect of training and airport improvements.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Explain an opportunity cost of advertising grants.

parts.label: g
parts.prompt: Using the information and your knowledge of economics, evaluate advertising grants as a way of improving the economy's performance during the tourism recovery.

steps.text: Value of final domestic output adjusted for price-level changes.
It is measured at constant/base-year prices.
People without work who are available for employment.
They are actively seeking work under the stated labour-force measure.
660 billion crowns at base-year prices.
660 billion / 22 million.
Convert billion/million to 1000 crowns per person.
30 000 crowns per person.
Label macro axes, AD1/AD2 and SRAS.
Shift AD right, increasing real output and the price level.
Visitor spending is an export of services.
Spare capacity permits a substantial initial real-output response.
Staff and transport bottlenecks limit expansion.
Unit costs can rise as scarce resources are bid up.
The economy moves onto a steeper effective AS range.
Additional demand then produces proportionately more price pressure and less real output.
Label two outputs and an outward PPC, or real output/price level and LRAS1/LRAS2.
Show a rise in productive potential.
Better skills and capital increase sustainable capacity.
It takes time, and projects need demand and efficient operation.
Government funds are scarce.
The same funds could improve training, transport or other public services.
The next best benefit forgone is the opportunity cost.
At capacity, advertising may stimulate demand without addressing the main supply constraint.

Indicative model reasoning (not an additive checklist): Advertising may help during spare capacity but is less useful when bottlenecks dominate. Compare additional demand with training/infrastructure, import leakages, congestion and fiscal cost. Evaluate timing and whether public grants create demand beyond what private firms would fund.
Variant-specific evaluation: Eligibility, access and distributional effects should be assessed rather than assuming all intended beneficiaries are reached.

A suitable diagram is helpful but is not a separate requirement for the top band in this evaluative response. Any conclusion must follow the student's evidence and assumptions.

title: Youth employment and skills mismatch — Jorven
stem:
All values and descriptions are fictional, constructed for practice. Jorven: Employers advertise technical vacancies while unemployed young people lack the required qualifications. The authority offers apprenticeships and considers a general cut in interest rates. Travel between rural homes and training centres is costly.

The following accounting data relate to the same year.

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Nominal GDP (billion crowns) | 660 |
| GDP deflator (base year=100) | 110 |
| Population (million) | 20 |

Show working. Give exact answers or round to two decimal places, retaining units.

A further case detail: The public budget is tight and service providers cannot expand capacity immediately.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt:
(i) Define real GDP. [2]

(ii) Define unemployment. [2]

parts.label: b
parts.prompt:
(i) Calculate real GDP. [2]

(ii) Calculate real GDP per capita in crowns per person. [3]

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why unemployment can coexist with unfilled vacancies.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Using a labour-market or capacity diagram, explain the purpose of training.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Using an AD/AS diagram, explain the intended effect of an interest-rate cut.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Explain why rural travel support may be complementary to training.

parts.label: g
parts.prompt: Using the information and your knowledge of economics, evaluate apprenticeships as a response to youth unemployment.

steps.text: Value of final domestic output adjusted for price-level changes.
It is measured at constant/base-year prices.
People without work who are available for employment.
They are actively seeking work under the stated labour-force measure.
600 billion crowns at base-year prices.
600 billion / 20 million.
Convert billion/million to 1000 crowns per person.
30 000 crowns per person.
Applicants' skills do not match required qualifications.
This is structural unemployment.
Firms cannot readily use those workers in the available jobs.
Raising total demand alone may leave the mismatch unresolved.
Label a relevant labour supply/demand diagram or LRAS with macro axes.
Show improved effective skilled labour supply or higher productive capacity.
Training raises relevant human capital.
It can improve matching and productivity if employers use the acquired skills.
Label macro axes and AD1/AD2/SRAS.
Shift AD right.
Cheaper borrowing may raise investment and consumption.
But more demand does not directly supply missing technical qualifications.
Attendance requires access to the training centre.
High transport cost can deter low-income participants.
Support lowers a non-tuition barrier and raises feasible participation.
It is effective only if courses and placements themselves are relevant.

Indicative model reasoning (not an additive checklist): Use vacancies, qualifications and travel costs to explain why matched apprenticeships target the stated structural cause. Assess placement quality, dropout, employer participation and lags. Compare general demand support and transport assistance; avoid assuming that a qualification guarantees employment.
Variant-specific evaluation: Timing, opportunity cost and short-run supply constraints qualify the scale of benefits.

title: Fiscal stimulus with import leakages — Arden
stem:
All values are constructed for Arden. A fixed-price Keynesian model gives MPS=0.20, MPM=0.20 and MPT=0.10; k=1/(MPS+MPM+MPT). The recessionary output gap is 60 billion crowns. Government debt is 400 billion and initial GDP is 800 billion. Borrowing cost is 3% annually. The government can finance spending through borrowing, but some projects take two years to start.

Part(a) totals 20 marks; part(b) is a 10-mark policy recommendation. Show working; give exact values or round to two decimal places.

Implementation evidence: Implementation can be phased and audited before nationwide expansion.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate the multiplier.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the autonomous spending increase needed to close the gap and state one assumption needed for this model result.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: Calculate initial debt/GDP and the annual interest on the additional borrowing.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt: Calculate the multiplier if MPM rises to 0.30 and the resulting output increase from the same spending.

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: Explain two limits of relying on this calculation to time a recovery.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Recommend a fiscal response to the output gap, using the quantitative evidence and implementation constraints.

Indicative model reasoning (not an additive checklist): Use the multiplier, required spending, interest bill and higher-import scenario. Weigh debt service, crowding out, imports and timing, accepting another well justified mix.
Variant-specific recommendation: Compare a monitored pilot with immediate broad rollout, using the quantitative evidence and acknowledging the cost of delay.

title: Fiscal stimulus with import leakages — Caldin
stem:
All values are constructed for Caldin. A fixed-price Keynesian model gives MPS=0.40, MPM=0.20 and MPT=0.10; k=1/(MPS+MPM+MPT). The recessionary output gap is 84 billion crowns. Government debt is 480 billion and initial GDP is 960 billion. Borrowing cost is 3% annually. The government can finance spending through borrowing, but some projects take two years to start.

Part(a) totals 20 marks; part(b) is a 10-mark policy recommendation. Show working; give exact values or round to two decimal places.

Implementation evidence: Benefits arrive with a lag, while some affected households need immediate assistance.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate the multiplier.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the autonomous spending increase needed to close the gap and state one assumption needed for this model result.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: Calculate initial debt/GDP and the annual interest on the additional borrowing.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt: Calculate the multiplier if MPM rises to 0.30 and the resulting output increase from the same spending.

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: Explain two limits of relying on this calculation to time a recovery.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Recommend a fiscal response to the output gap, using the quantitative evidence and implementation constraints.

steps.text: 58.80 billion crowns.
This assumes fixed prices, spare capacity, unchanged propensities and no offsetting policy response.
1.76 billion crowns per year.
73.50 billion crowns.
Project approval/construction can be delayed.
Spending may arrive after the downturn has ended.
Capacity constraints can then turn part of the demand increase into inflation.
Propensities and confidence can change during the downturn.
Imports and saving may differ from the assumed coefficients.
The forecast is conditional rather than a guaranteed output gain.

Prioritize timely useful maintenance or transfers where projects are delayed; compare automatic stabilizers and larger infrastructure for later capacity. Variant-specific recommendation: Compare transitional support with the main structural policy, recognizing fiscal cost and avoiding unsupported promises of immediate benefits.

title: Tax schedules and redistribution — Elarin
stem:
The following case is fictional in Elarin. Income is 50 thousand crowns annually. The first 10 thousand is tax-free, the next 20 thousand taxed at 20%, and income above 30 thousand at 40%. Apply rates by band. A representative expenditure of 12 thousand crowns excludes a 15% consumption tax. Quintile income shares before a proposed reform are 5%,10%,15%,25%,45%; after the reform the projected shares are 8%,12%,17%,25%,38%. Tax administration is imperfect and rural services are weak.

Part(a) totals 20 marks; part(b) is a 10-mark policy recommendation. Show working; give exact values or round to two decimal places.

Implementation evidence: Implementation can be phased and audited before nationwide expansion.

parts.label: a(ii)

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: State the cumulative income shares at cumulative population shares 20%,40%,60%,80% before and after reform.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt:

(ii) Explain the indicated change in income inequality. [2]

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: Explain why equalizing income shares need not by itself eliminate multidimensional poverty.

parts.label: b

title: A weighted price index and inflation policy — Ilyra
subtopic: A weighted price index and inflation policy
stem:
A fictional fixed basket for Ilyra contains the quantities below; these are base-year quantities.

| Item | Base quantity | Base price (crowns) | Current price (crowns) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Food | 4 | 10 | 12 |
| Transport | 2 | 20 | 21 |
| Other goods | 8 | 5 | 6 |

Imported fuel costs explain much of the transport increase. The policy rate is 6%; expected inflation for the interest calculation is 4%. Use the approximate relation: real interest rate = nominal rate minus expected inflation. Real output is below potential and some firms have weak cash flow.

Part(a) totals 20 marks; part(b) is a 10-mark policy recommendation. Show working; give exact values or round to two decimal places.

Implementation evidence: Implementation can be phased and audited before nationwide expansion.

parts.prompt: Calculate the cost of the basket in the base and current years.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the current weighted price index, base year 100, and inflation since the base year.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: Calculate food's base expenditure weight and the expected real interest rate.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt: Explain two limitations of this basket as a measure of every household's inflation.

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: Using AD/AS analysis, explain a trade-off of raising interest rates after the fuel shock.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Recommend a response to inflation that considers the output and distributional consequences.

title: Debt dynamics and stabilization — Merin
stem:
This constructed case concerns Merin. Initial debt is 300 billion crowns and nominal GDP is 600 billion. The next year's overall budget deficit, including interest, is 24 billion. Interest on initial debt averages 4%. Assume no other debt changes. Nominal GDP is projected to grow 3%. Some borrowing finances maintenance of schools; tax collection is weak.

Part(a) totals 20 marks; part(b) is a 10-mark policy recommendation. Show working; give exact values or round to two decimal places.

Implementation evidence: Implementation can be phased and audited before nationwide expansion.

parts.prompt: Calculate the projected end-year debt and GDP.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: Calculate projected debt/GDP and its percentage-point change.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt: Explain the distinction between a deficit and debt.

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: Explain two reasons a ratio alone cannot establish whether debt is sustainable.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Recommend a fiscal approach that balances stabilization, public services and debt sustainability.
